paragraphs: This paper studies when an algorithm can recover every community membership in a randomly generated graph. Its setting is a binary symmetric stochastic block model: vertices belong to two equally sized groups, and connections are more likely within groups than between them. The goal is exact recovery, rather than merely finding a partition that is mostly correct.

The proposed algorithm has two stages. It first runs the power method from a random starting point, then switches to a generalized power method that identifies the communities after finitely many iterations. This combines an initial iterative calculation with a second procedure directed toward the discrete community assignment.

The guarantee applies when connection probabilities have the specified logarithmic scaling and the fixed parameters satisfy sqrt(alpha) − sqrt(beta) > sqrt(2). Under that condition, recovery succeeds with probability approaching one as the graph grows, using nearly linear time up to logarithmic factors. Numerical results support the theory. The contribution connects a sharp statistical recovery threshold with a computationally efficient procedure for this particular graph model.
icml-2020-a-nearly-linear-time-algorithm.tldr: A two-stage iterative algorithm exactly recovers communities in a specified stochastic block model in nearly linear time above its recovery threshold.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models explain observed data through hidden structure, but learning their parameters by exact maximum likelihood is often computationally intractable. A common response is to approximate the posterior distribution of the hidden variables. This paper explores a different route: learning a function that directly estimates the parameter updates needed for maximum-likelihood learning.

The method, called amortised learning, uses a wake-sleep Monte Carlo strategy to train that update estimator. Its central requirement is that the generative model can simulate both hidden variables and observations. The model can therefore be treated as a black box for generating the examples used by the learning procedure.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness across complex models, including models with discrete hidden variables and hidden variables on non-Euclidean spaces. These examples matter because the approach is not confined to one familiar type of latent representation. The contribution is an alternative target for approximation: learn the updates used to fit the model, rather than first constructing an approximate posterior over its hidden variables.
icml-2020-amortised-learning-by-wake-sle.tldr: Amortised learning uses simulated data and a wake-sleep strategy to learn maximum-likelihood parameter updates directly.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to estimate the long-run behavior of an ergodic Markov chain from a fixed collection of transitions. Unlike simulation-based approaches, the learner cannot return to the underlying system and gather longer trajectories. The available transitions may also have been collected by a separate procedure whose details are unknown.

The proposed estimator recovers a correction ratio function over the recorded data. That correction is the basis for estimating properties of the stationary distribution despite the way the batch was collected. The authors develop this idea into a variational power method and prove that its estimates are consistent under general conditions.

Consistency gives the approach a theoretical foundation for recovering the desired quantities as the available information grows under those conditions. The method also unifies approaches from several research areas. Empirically, it produces substantially better estimates across the reported problems, including queueing, stochastic differential equations, processing existing Markov chain Monte Carlo output, and off-policy evaluation. Its practical relevance lies in extracting long-run information when further interaction with the system is unavailable.
icml-2020-batch-stationary-distribution-.tldr: A variational power method estimates stationary-distribution properties from a fixed transition batch without further access to the system.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows. This paper addresses that challenge by exploiting symmetry among agents. It studies a mean-field formulation, where a state describes a distribution over a continuous space, shifting the learning problem toward the collective population representation.

The proposed MF-FQI algorithm represents these distributions through their mean embeddings and uses that representation to solve the mean-field reinforcement learning problem. This is the key connection between the population-level formulation and a learning algorithm: distributions themselves become the objects on which the method operates. The paper also provides a non-asymptotic analysis, addressing performance without relying only on an infinite-data limit.

A highlighted finding is that observing more agents improves MF-FQI's performance in this setting. The authors describe this as a beneficial effect of having many agents, reversing the usual concern that additional agents only make learning harder. The result concerns the symmetric mean-field problem studied here; its significance is that population size can supply useful information to an algorithm designed around distributions.
icml-2020-breaking-the-curse-of-many-age.tldr: MF-FQI uses distribution embeddings to learn in mean-field multi-agent systems, with performance improving as more agents are observed.

paragraphs: Unobserved factors can distort causal estimates when they influence both treatment and outcome. This paper focuses on factors shared across observations. For example, students receiving individual educational interventions may also share the influence of their course's difficulty. Such grouping gives the hidden confounding a structure that a model can explicitly represent.

The authors introduce GP-SLC, a hierarchical Bayesian model using Gaussian processes with structured latent confounders. They pair it with a Monte Carlo inference algorithm based on elliptical slice sampling. The model allows flexible relationships among confounders, measured covariates, treatment, and outcome, requiring minimal assumptions about the functional forms of those relationships.

GP-SLC provides Bayesian uncertainty estimates for individual treatment effects, making uncertainty part of the causal estimate itself. Across three benchmark datasets, it is competitive with or more accurate than widely used causal inference methods. The examples include infant development and temperature effects on regional energy consumption. These findings support modeling shared hidden influences as a useful route to improving causal estimates in the studied settings.
icml-2020-causal-inference-using-gaussia.tldr: GP-SLC models shared hidden confounders with Gaussian processes to estimate individual treatment effects and their Bayesian uncertainty.

paragraphs: Predicting an outcome and knowing how to change it are different tasks. This paper addresses the second: identifying causal effects so that interventions can guide decisions. Although a known causal structure can enable causal reasoning through do-calculus, learning an entire structure from observational data is difficult in many applications.

The authors study a restricted observation setting in which only the response variable can be observed under intervention. Their approach actively chooses a limited set of interventions to identify causal effects cost-effectively. Intervention selection is therefore part of the learning strategy, rather than simply accepting whichever experimental observations happen to be available.

Theoretical analysis and empirical studies support the proposed approach's effectiveness. The contribution matters because it connects limited experimental access with a decision-focused objective: learning the effects needed to influence an outcome. Its stated scope is specifically the setting where intervention outcomes are observable through the response variable. Within that setting, the work offers a strategy for making a limited intervention budget informative about causal effects.
icml-2020-cost-effectively-identifying-c.tldr: An active intervention strategy identifies causal effects cost-effectively when only the response variable is observable under intervention.

paragraphs: Using several source datasets to learn for a different target dataset creates a tradeoff. Additional data can help, but sources that differ too much from the target can harm training. This paper studies how to combine sources systematically, addressing a gap between practical aggregation methods and theoretical justification.

The authors derive a finite-sample generalization bound based on discrepancies between domains. They use that bound to motivate an optimization procedure called Domain AggRegation Network, or DARN. During training, DARN automatically adjusts the balance between including more data to increase the effective sample size and excluding irrelevant data that could have negative effects.

Experiments show that DARN can substantially outperform the compared state-of-the-art alternatives on multiple real-world tasks, including digit recognition, object recognition, and sentiment analysis. The findings support adaptive source combination in these settings. The broader contribution is a connection between an explicit generalization argument and a practical training procedure, giving the data-volume-versus-relevance tradeoff a central role in how multiple sources are used.
icml-2020-domain-aggregation-networks-fo.tldr: DARN uses a generalization bound to dynamically balance source-data quantity against relevance when adapting to a target domain.

paragraphs: This paper studies how important a variable is for prediction at the population level, together with how uncertain that importance estimate is. Such information can help researchers understand the data-generating process and decide which measurements to collect. The target quantity is the Shapley Population Variable Importance Measure, abbreviated SPVIM.

Computing the true measure has complexity that grows exponentially with the number of variables. The authors instead estimate it by randomly sampling a number of feature subsets proportional to the number of observations. This sampling strategy makes it possible to approach the population-level importance question without evaluating the full collection of feature subsets.

The estimator converges at an asymptotically optimal rate. The authors also derive its asymptotic distribution, enabling confidence intervals and hypothesis tests with the stated statistical validity. Simulations show good finite-sample performance. In an in-hospital mortality prediction task, different machine learning algorithms produce similar importance estimates. Together, these results support computationally efficient importance estimation accompanied by statistical uncertainty, rather than an importance score alone.
icml-2020-efficient-nonparametric-statis.tldr: Randomly sampled feature subsets enable efficient estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests for population-level Shapley variable importance.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models are useful when predictive uncertainty matters, but using that uncertainty can require sampling from a posterior distribution. Those samples support Monte Carlo calculations of quantities that are otherwise intractable. This paper targets the sampling cost: existing accurate approaches can scale cubically with the number of locations where a function is evaluated.

The authors identify a decomposition that separates the Gaussian process prior from the contribution of the observed data. They build a general-purpose posterior sampling method around that separation. The approach also works with sparse approximations, connecting efficient sampling at test time with techniques that make training scalable.

Experiments examine both the statistical properties of competing sampling schemes and their practical consequences. The reported results show that the proposed decoupled sample paths represent Gaussian process posteriors accurately at a fraction of the usual computational cost. The contribution addresses a distinct bottleneck from fitting the model: efficiently drawing functions so that posterior uncertainty can be used within larger computational procedures.
icml-2020-efficiently-sampling-functions.tldr: Separating prior and data contributions enables accurate Gaussian process posterior function sampling at substantially reduced empirical cost.

paragraphs: Bayesian deep learning often aims to approximate a neural network's posterior distribution more accurately. This paper questions whether that posterior necessarily gives the best predictive target in the popular networks studied. The authors use careful Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to investigate predictive performance, rather than assuming that more faithful posterior approximation will improve predictions.

Their experiments find that predictions induced by the Bayes posterior are systematically worse than those from simpler methods, including point estimates learned with stochastic gradient descent. They also find substantial improvements from a cold posterior, which gives the observed evidence more weight than standard Bayesian updating does.

The authors propose several possible explanations for this cold-posterior effect and evaluate them experimentally. Their argument is that understanding why modified posteriors predict better deserves attention alongside improving inference algorithms. The findings challenge the predictive value of the standard posterior in the investigated settings; they do not establish that Bayesian inference is universally inferior. The central issue is whether the distribution being approximated is itself an effective predictive choice.
icml-2020-how-good-is-the-bayes-posterio.tldr: Careful sampling finds poorer predictions from standard Bayes posteriors in the studied neural networks and substantial gains from cold posteriors.

paragraphs: This paper studies extrapolation: making useful inferences beyond the range of experiences represented in training data. The authors distinguish this from interpolation among training examples. Their focus is on learning representations that support the more demanding task of reasoning outside the domain covered by previous observations.

They introduce a visual analogy benchmark that measures extrapolation in degrees. Evaluation depends on how far a case lies from the convex domain defined by the training data, making distance beyond that domain an explicit part of the test. They also propose temporal context normalization, a simple technique intended to encourage representations that emphasize relationships among objects.

The reported experiments show a substantial improvement in extrapolation, with temporal context normalization considerably outperforming several competitive techniques. This supports the usefulness of relational representations on the introduced task. The benchmark and method address complementary needs: measuring how performance changes beyond the training domain, and changing learned representations to help with that challenge. The findings concern the demonstrated extrapolation ability rather than a universal guarantee of reasoning outside training experience.
icml-2020-learning-representations-that-.tldr: A graded visual analogy benchmark shows that temporal context normalization substantially improves extrapolation by encouraging relational representations.

paragraphs: Automated searches over hyperparameters and neural architectures can be expensive because they train many candidate models. This paper aims to save computation by stopping poor candidates early. The challenge is deciding which training runs are unpromising when only limited information about their learning progress has been observed.

The authors frame this decision as a ranking and transfer learning problem. Their model optimizes a pairwise ranking loss and uses learning curves from other datasets. The desired output is a useful ordering of candidate curves. Qualitative results show that the model can rank effectively without requiring many observed curves or long training histories.

In a neural architecture search experiment, the method achieves acceleration of up to a factor of 100 without significant degradation in the discovered architecture's performance. Further experiments examine ranking quality, individual model components, and predictive behavior. The reported speedup is an experimental result rather than a guarantee for every search. The contribution is a way to reuse prior training experience to make earlier computational allocation decisions.
icml-2020-learning-to-rank-learning-curv.tldr: Learning to rank partial training curves across datasets enables early stopping and speeds up the reported architecture search by up to 100 times.

paragraphs: This paper develops model-free reinforcement learning algorithms for continuing decision problems evaluated by average reward. The infinite-horizon setting has no fixed final step, so the objective concerns sustained performance. The authors seek algorithms that retain the memory and computational advantages associated with model-free learning while providing theoretical regret guarantees.

The first algorithm converts the average-reward problem into a discounted-reward problem. Under the assumption that the Markov decision process is weakly communicating, it achieves regret of order T^(2/3) after T steps. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first model-free algorithm for general Markov decision processes in this setting.

The second algorithm draws on adaptive methods for adversarial multi-armed bandits and improves the regret rate to order sqrt(T). That stronger rate requires the stronger assumption of ergodicity. It improves on the previously available model-free rate of order T^(3/4) for the ergodic setting. The two results therefore offer different combinations of assumptions and guarantees, rather than a single bound that applies equally broadly.
icml-2020-model-free-reinforcement-learn.tldr: Two model-free algorithms achieve sublinear regret for average-reward learning, with a stronger rate available under a stronger ergodic assumption.

paragraphs: A neural network controlling a physical system faces a different robustness question from a predictor used once: disturbances can persist while the controller and system repeatedly influence each other. This paper combines static neural network certification methods with robust control theory to study that closed-loop setting.

The authors give a sufficient condition and an algorithm for certifying that state and control constraints remain satisfied under persistent perturbations bounded in the infinity norm. The approach finds a positively invariant set, meaning a region the closed-loop dynamics continue to stay within. This construction does not require the neural network policy to be continuous.

The paper also develops an attack strategy that substantially outperforms exhaustive Monte Carlo search in the reported evaluation. Its certification algorithm works well on learned models and can achieve a fivefold improvement over a traditional Lipschitz-based method on cart-pole balance control. The certification condition is sufficient, so the result establishes robustness when that condition is met; it does not claim that every robust controller must satisfy it.
icml-2020-neural-network-control-policy-.tldr: Invariant-set analysis provides sufficient robustness certificates for neural controllers facing persistent infinity-norm-bounded adversarial disturbances.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed data can violate assumptions used by existing differentially private optimization methods, undermining their privacy guarantees. This paper studies private stochastic convex optimization under such irregular data across several settings. Its guarantees concern excess population risk: how much worse the learned solution is than the population objective's optimum.

For strongly convex, smooth losses, a sample-and-aggregate method achieves a bound scaling as d^3/(n epsilon^4), suppressing logarithmic and other factors. Here d is dimension, n is sample size, and epsilon is the privacy parameter. With additional loss assumptions, an alternative result improves expected excess risk to a scaling of d^2/(n epsilon^2).

A gradient smoothing and trimming scheme removes those additional conditions and gives high-probability bounds scaling as d^2/(n epsilon^2) for strongly convex losses and d^(2/3)/(n epsilon^2)^(1/3) for general convex losses, again suppressing factors. The distinction between expected and high-probability guarantees matters when comparing these results. Experiments on synthetic and real data suggest that the algorithms effectively handle the irregularity motivating the work.
icml-2020-on-differentially-private-stoc.tldr: Private optimization methods based on aggregation, smoothing, and trimming provide risk guarantees for heavy-tailed data under several convexity settings.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles can change their predictions under small input perturbations. This paper extends robustness verification and certified defense beyond infinity-norm perturbations to general p-norm constraints. The difficulty is that these constraints require accounting for relationships among perturbations across features, even though individual tree nodes make decisions using one feature at a time.

For ensembles of decision stumps, the authors prove that complete verification is NP-complete for finite positive p, while polynomial-time algorithms exist for p equal to zero or infinity. They develop an efficient dynamic programming method for sound verification in the finite-positive-p setting. Sound verification supplies valid certificates without claiming complete verification of every case.

For ensembles of larger trees, the paper extends an existing multilevel verification algorithm to general p-norm perturbations. It also introduces what the authors describe as the first certified defense for training these ensembles under such perturbations, with empirical validation on real datasets. The contribution combines a computational difficulty result with verification and training methods that address the broader perturbation setting.
icml-2020-on-lp-norm-robustness-of-ensem.tldr: The paper characterizes the difficulty of general p-norm robustness verification and develops sound verification and certified training methods for tree ensembles.

paragraphs: Reporting confidence intervals for selected results creates a collective uncertainty problem. The relevant error measure is the false coverage rate: the expected fraction of reported intervals that fail to contain their corresponding parameters. This paper studies control of that rate when parameters arrive sequentially over time.

The setting allows an infinite sequence of fixed, unknown parameters. The authors propose a framework that requires the scientist to be able to construct marginal confidence intervals. Its purpose is to manage error across the selected intervals reported throughout the sequence, making the reporting process itself part of the statistical problem.

The framework also yields online false discovery rate procedures and methods for classifying parameter signs while controlling the false sign rate. The same methodology applies to prediction intervals, with implications for selective conformal inference. These connections matter because selection affects more than hypothesis testing: it also affects which intervals and directional conclusions become visible. The paper provides a shared approach to controlling these related reporting errors as results accumulate.
icml-2020-online-control-of-the-false-co.tldr: An online framework controls errors among selected confidence intervals and also yields false discovery and false sign rate procedures.

paragraphs: Autoregressive models can perform well at likelihood-based modeling while remaining slow to sample from. This paper addresses that practical mismatch. Neural implementations are generally designed to support fast inference, and the authors ask how that existing capability can be used to accelerate sample generation while leaving the underlying model intact.

Their predictive sampling algorithm has two variants. One uses fixed-point iteration with the autoregressive model; the other uses learned forecasting modules. Both are presented as ways to improve the sampling procedure, preserving the model that defines the distribution being used.

The authors evaluate the methods in explicit likelihood modeling and in modeling discrete latent variables within an autoencoder. The experiments span the listed image datasets, including binary MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10, and Imagenet32 across those settings. They report considerable reductions in autoregressive inference calls and improvements in sampling speed relative to the evaluated baselines. The contribution makes the distinction between modeling quality and generation cost concrete: a sampling procedure can improve practical usability without replacing the trained model.
icml-2020-predictive-sampling-with-forec.tldr: Predictive sampling accelerates autoregressive generation using fixed-point iteration or learned forecasting while keeping the underlying model intact.

paragraphs: When one agent chooses data for another agent to learn from, the choice can reflect a shared goal. This paper studies that cooperative situation: both agents want the learner to infer the intended hypothesis. The data-selection process is therefore part of the inference problem, with cooperation explicitly built into the relationship between the agents.

The authors develop theoretical approaches for analyzing Sequential Cooperative Bayesian Inference, where learning proceeds through successive observations. They examine consistency, convergence rate, and stability. These address complementary questions: whether learning approaches the intended conclusion, how rapidly it progresses, and how robust the process is.

The analysis supports cooperation as a theoretically grounded inference mechanism, extending beyond demonstrations that cooperative behavior is merely possible. Its focus on effectiveness, sample efficiency, and robustness connects the shared-goal assumption to the quality of learning over time. The paper also discusses implications for cooperation between people and between humans and machines. Its conclusions concern Bayesian agents in the cooperative framework studied, where the data selector and learner share the intended inferential goal.
icml-2020-sequential-cooperative-bayesia.tldr: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for sequential Bayesian learning when the data selector and learner cooperate toward the same hypothesis.

paragraphs: This paper brings several approximate Bayesian inference methods into one framework for temporal and spatio-temporal Gaussian process models. It addresses non-conjugate models, where the inference problem requires approximation. The central formulation expresses inference as a simple parameter update performed during Kalman smoothing.

From this viewpoint, expectation propagation, variational inference, and classical Kalman smoothers become closely connected procedures. The authors show that replacing the moment-matching step in power expectation propagation with linearisation recovers classical smoothers, including extended and unscented variants. This identifies a concrete algorithmic relationship among methods that can otherwise appear separate.

The framework also supports combining the benefits of expectation propagation's cavity distribution with the computational efficiency of linearisation. Extensive empirical analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of different algorithms within this unified view, and the authors provide fast implementations in JAX. The contribution is both explanatory and practical: it clarifies which update choices distinguish the methods and uses that connection to construct efficient inference schemes for the temporal models under study.
icml-2020-state-space-expectation-propag.tldr: A Kalman-smoothing update framework unifies temporal Gaussian process inference methods and combines expectation propagation with efficient linearisation.

paragraphs: This paper seeks simple off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithms with strong continuous-control performance. It begins by examining Soft Actor-Critic, which uses entropy maximization. The authors demonstrate that its entropy term addresses action saturation associated with bounded action spaces, identifying a specific problem that a simpler mechanism might address.

They propose streamlined alternatives using either a normalization scheme or inverted gradients. In the reported experiments, both can match Soft Actor-Critic's sample efficiency without entropy maximization. The authors then introduce a non-uniform method for choosing transitions from the replay buffer, changing which stored experiences are emphasized during learning.

Extensive experiments show that the sampling scheme achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency on the challenging continuous-control tasks evaluated. The findings are combined into Streamlined Off Policy with Emphasizing Recent Experience, with public-domain code provided. The contribution links two practical choices—handling bounded actions and selecting replay data—to strong empirical performance. It supports a simpler algorithmic design in these benchmarks without establishing that entropy maximization is unnecessary for every reinforcement learning problem.
icml-2020-striving-for-simplicity-and-pe.tldr: Simple action handling and replay sampling match or improve benchmark sample efficiency while streamlining off-policy continuous-control learning.

paragraphs: Dropout is widely used to regularize neural networks, but this paper argues that its influence has two distinct components. One is explicit: dropout changes the training objective after averaging over its randomness. The other is implicit: randomness in the training updates changes the learning process itself.

The authors connect this implicit component to the regularizing effect of stochasticity in small-minibatch stochastic gradient descent. They use controlled experiments to disentangle the two dropout effects, which are normally intertwined during training. This distinction matters because examining only the average objective leaves out an additional source of regularization.

The paper then derives simplified analytic expressions for both effects in deep neural networks, using derivatives of the model and the loss. In practical evaluations, these analytic regularizers capture the important aspects of dropout and can faithfully replace it. The findings provide a more detailed explanation of dropout's behavior: both the objective being optimized and the randomness of the optimization updates contribute to the regularization observed in the studied networks.
icml-2020-the-implicit-and-explicit-regu.tldr: Dropout regularizes through both its expected objective and stochastic updates, and analytic regularizers can reproduce these effects in practice.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling uses posterior uncertainty to balance exploring uncertain options with choosing options that appear rewarding. Neural approaches often represent that uncertainty through global variables. This paper proposes a probabilistic framework in which uncertainty in local latent variables instead supplies the sampled mean rewards used for decision making.

The authors approximate the local-variable posterior with variational inference. They then introduce a semi-implicit structure to make that approximation more expressive. The modeling choice places the source of exploration in the local uncertainty representation, providing an alternative to the global-variable uncertainty used by many Bayesian neural approaches.

Experiments on eight contextual bandit benchmark datasets show state-of-the-art performance together with low computational complexity. These findings support local uncertainty as an effective guide for Thompson sampling on the evaluated tasks. The significance is that the representation of uncertainty is itself a design decision: the paper changes where uncertainty enters reward sampling and reports strong results without requiring the same global uncertainty formulation as the methods motivating the work.
icml-2020-thompson-sampling-via-local-un.tldr: Thompson sampling driven by local latent uncertainty achieves strong contextual bandit benchmark performance with low computational complexity.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness requires predictions to remain unchanged within a specified range of input perturbations. Methods enforcing this property can reduce performance on natural examples. This paper investigates that degradation through regularization, asking how the push toward robust predictions changes the internal behavior of a neural network.

The authors identify quantities from neural network generalization analysis and study them empirically. They find that adversarial robustness biases networks toward less confident solutions by making feature-space changes smoother, uniformly across directions, in most layers. Such smoothing can help prevent abrupt prediction changes when inputs are perturbed.

Their analysis also associates this smoothing with samples becoming concentrated around decision boundaries, producing lower confidence and worse standard performance. The findings offer an empirical explanation for the observed degradation in the studied networks. They suggest considering gentler ways of incorporating robustness to avoid the problematic regularization. This is a proposed research direction based on the observations, rather than a demonstrated method that eliminates the accuracy cost in every setting.
icml-2020-towards-understanding-the-regu.tldr: Empirical analysis links adversarial robustness to feature smoothing and reduced confidence, helping explain degraded performance on natural examples.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play imaging methods combine an optimization procedure with a denoiser that supplies prior information about images. Although effective in practice, they often require manual parameter adjustment across imaging conditions and scene content. This paper develops a method that automatically chooses internal parameters, including the penalty parameter, denoising strength, and stopping time.

The central component is a policy network that searches for parameter choices. It is trained using a mixture of model-free and model-based deep reinforcement learning. The learned policy can choose different parameters for different states of the reconstruction process, making parameter selection responsive to the current problem-solving situation.

Numerical and visual experiments show that these choices are often more efficient and effective than existing handcrafted criteria. The authors also examine practical denoiser considerations; together with the policy, these yield state-of-the-art results on the evaluated linear and nonlinear inverse imaging problems. Compressed sensing MRI and phase retrieval provide promising examples. The findings support replacing repeated manual tuning with a learned policy in the demonstrated reconstruction settings.
icml-2020-tuning-free-plug-and-play-prox.tldr: A reinforcement-learned policy automatically selects plug-and-play reconstruction parameters and stopping times, improving results on the evaluated imaging problems.
